study_identification.title: Dissecting Heterogeneity in Functional Network Connectivity Aberrations in Antipsychotic Medication-Naïve First Episode Psychosis Patients - A Normative Modeling Study

study_characteristics.study_objective: To characterize inter-individual heterogeneity in functional networks in antipsychotic medication-naïve first-episode psychosis patients and investigate if normative values can be leveraged to identify biologically less heterogeneous subgroups of patients.

preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: T1-weighted images were skull-stripped using FSL BET. The first 10 volumes of each fMRI run were removed to allow for signal equilibration and then corrected for magnetic field inhomogeneities and integrated using FSL topup. Functional images were then imported into the CONN toolbox (version 21a) where they were corrected for slice timing and motion using rigid-body alignment, co-registered to the skull-stripped structural image, normalized to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space to allow for later parcellation using the Yeo-17 atlas, bandpass filtered (0.008 Hz - 0.08 Hz), and spatially smoothed with a 4-mm full width at half maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel. Outlier volumes were censored using the artifact detection (ART) toolbox (composite volume-to-volume motion >0.9 mm and global signal intensity >5SDs). Framewise displacement and percentage of censored data were then calculated to determine if scans should be excluded from analysis; scans with a mean framewise displacement >2mm or had >50% of censored data were excluded. The six motion parameters derived from rigid-body realignment and their derivatives, as well as the first component time series derived from cerebrospinal fluid and white matter using aCompCor and corresponding derivatives, were regressed out from the signal. Global signal regression was not performed as this processing step has been shown to introduce false negative correlations. Functional brain networks were then parcellated using the Yeo-17 functional network parcellation atlas, resulting in a functional connectivity matrix of 136 connectivity values. During post-processing quality control, if processed resting-state fMRI images were found to not have correctly co-registered to the structural image or normalized to the MNI space, the registration algorithm, Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs), was used to correct the registration mistakes.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Descriptive analysis of heterogeneity: percentage of patients sharing deviations in same functional connections; Post hoc subgroup analysis: patients grouped by deviation profiles (positive only, negative only, mixed, none); Z-test to compare within-subgroup deviation similarity to overall group; FDR correction with α=0.05; Subgroup comparisons for clinical variables (BPRS, RBANS) using ANOVA and chi-square tests (Supplemental Table 1)
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Functional connectivity deviations in first-episode psychosis are highly heterogeneous, with no more than 11.1% of patients sharing deviations in the same network connections, and 48% showing no significant deviations; subgroups based on deviation profiles (positive only, negative only, mixed, none) are biologically less heterogeneous than the overall group.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: This study used normative modeling to characterize individual-level resting-state functional network pathology in 108 antipsychotic medication-naïve first-episode psychosis patients. Key findings include: (1) High inter-individual heterogeneity, with no more than 11.1% of patients sharing positive deviations and 8.3% sharing negative deviations in the same network connections. (2) Approximately 48% of patients showed no significant functional connectivity deviations (threshold ±2 SD). (3) Four theoretically plausible subgroups were identified: 25% had exclusively positive connectivity deviations, 24% had exclusively negative deviations, 2.8% had mixed deviations, and 48% had no significant deviations. (4) Subgroups showed significantly less heterogeneity than the overall group: the positive deviation group shared deviations in up to 40.7% of patients (z=3.66, p=0.0001), primarily between somatomotor A (SM-A) and higher cognitive networks (DAN-A, CCN-C, central visual, DMN-A); the negative deviation group shared deviations in up to 23.1% of patients (z=-2.15, p=0.016), most commonly between SM-A and limbic networks. (5) Subgroups did not differ in clinical presentation (BPRS scores) or cognitive function (RBANS scores), suggesting neurobiological heterogeneity is not reflected in clinical phenotypes.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The normative models likely overrepresent individuals with European ancestry and do not match the patient demographics (63.89% racial/ethnic minority), which is a major limitation as transferring models to diverse populations should be done with caution; the study only examined cortical functional networks using Yeo-17 parcellation and did not investigate subcortical connectivity; the mixed deviation subgroup was very small (N=3), limiting interpretability; this is a cross-sectional study and longitudinal stability of deviation profiles is unknown; generalizability requires independent replication in different first-episode psychosis cohorts.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This study demonstrates for the first time that normative modeling can identify biologically less heterogeneous subgroups of first-episode psychosis patients based on functional connectivity deviation profiles, despite these subgroups being clinically indistinguishable. The finding that 48% of patients show no significant functional connectivity deviations challenges conventional understanding of connectome pathology as a core feature of psychosis. The study suggests that different subgroups may have distinct pathophysiological mechanisms (neocortical vs limbic dysfunction) that converge on a similar clinical phenotype, which has important implications for precision psychiatry and treatment selection. The authors note the need for independent replication, longitudinal follow-up to assess stability of subtypes, and multi-level integration of structural, microstructural, and functional pathology.

general_notes.general_notes: This is a preprint (medRxiv) that has not been peer-reviewed. The paper was posted on August 23, 2024. The study is notable for being the first to apply normative modeling of resting-state networks to antipsychotic medication-naïve first-episode psychosis patients, which eliminates confounds of medication effects and illness chronicity. Cannabis use was not an exclusion criterion (41.67% of patients used cannabis) to maintain generalizability. The specific source/citation for the pre-trained normative model (trained on ~22,000 individuals) is not provided, which limits reproducibility. Race/ethnicity demographics show the patient sample was highly diverse (African American:63, Caucasian:39, Asian:4, Hispanic/Latino:1, Other:1) but the normative reference may not adequately represent this diversity. The study excluded patients with >5 days lifetime antipsychotic exposure. Imaging was acquired on a Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma 3T scanner. This study references and builds upon Rutherford et al. (2023, eLife) which demonstrated normative modeling utility in chronic schizophrenia.
